title: Integration
description: Connecting Salesforce with other systems: APIs, OAuth, callouts, custom endpoints, bulk data, events and the patterns that tie them together.

nodes.title: API fundamentals
nodes.summary: REST, SOAP, JSON, HTTP methods and status codes.
nodes.lesson:
Integration is systems talking over **APIs**:

- **REST** uses HTTP verbs on URLs: `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PATCH` updates, `DELETE` removes, with JSON bodies.
- **SOAP** sends XML envelopes described by a WSDL; older but still common in enterprises.
- **Status codes** say what happened: `200` OK, `201` created, `400` bad request, `401` not authenticated, `403` not allowed, `404` not found, `429` too many requests, `5xx` the server failed.
- Salesforce offers many APIs: REST, SOAP, Bulk, Metadata, Tooling, Streaming and Pub/Sub, each for a different job.
concepts: HTTP methods and what they mean
pitfalls: Treating every non-200 the same: retrying a 400 never helps, retrying a 503 often does.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method updates part of a record in Salesforce's REST API?
options: PUT with only the changed fields
quiz.why: PATCH updates the fields you send.

quiz.q: What does a 429 status mean?
options: Not found: the resource doesn't exist
quiz.why: 429 is rate limiting; back off and retry later.

quiz.q: Which Salesforce API is built for loading millions of records?
quiz.why: Bulk API processes large data sets asynchronously.

nodes.title: Connected apps and OAuth
nodes.summary: How other systems log in to Salesforce.
nodes.lesson:
External systems authenticate with **OAuth 2.0** through a **Connected App** (or External Client App) in Salesforce:

- **Web server flow** (with PKCE): a user logs in and approves; your server exchanges a one-time code for tokens. SFCode connects your org this way.
- **JWT bearer flow**: server-to-server, signed with a certificate; no user interaction.
- **Client credentials flow**: server-to-server with a client secret, running as a set integration user.
- **Scopes** limit what the token can do (`api`, `refresh_token`…). Use the narrowest set.
- Run integrations as a dedicated **integration user** with only the permissions it needs.
concepts: JWT bearer and client credentials for server-to-server
pitfalls: Integrations running as an admin's personal account.
Storing refresh tokens or secrets in plain text.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. What does Salesforce send back to your callback in step 3?
quiz.why: The code is exchanged server-side for tokens in step 4.
quiz.imageAlt: OAuth diagram, step 3: Salesforce redirects back with a one-time code.

quiz.q: Using the diagram, what does the app send to /token with the code?
options: Its client secret and the PKCE verifier
The user's password and username, to confirm
quiz.why: The secret and verifier prove the app is the one that started the flow.
quiz.imageAlt: OAuth diagram, step 4: app posts code, secret and PKCE verifier to /token.

quiz.q: A nightly server job must call Salesforce with no user present. Which flow fits?
quiz.why: Server-to-server flows need no user interaction.

nodes.diagramCaption: OAuth web server flow: redirect to authorize, user approves, callback with a code, code exchanged with secret and PKCE verifier for tokens.

nodes.title: Salesforce REST API
nodes.summary: Reading and writing records from outside.
nodes.lesson:
With a token, an external system calls `https://<instance>/services/data/vXX.X/...`:

- `GET /sobjects/Account/<id>` reads a record; `POST /sobjects/Account` creates; `PATCH` updates; `DELETE` deletes.
- `GET /query?q=SELECT+...` runs SOQL; large results come back in pages with `nextRecordsUrl`.
- **Composite** requests bundle several calls into one round trip, optionally all-or-none.
- Upsert by **external Id**: `PATCH /sobjects/Account/External_Id__c/12345`: create or update without knowing the Salesforce Id.
- Every call counts toward the org's daily API request limit.
pitfalls: One call per record for thousands of records: use composite or Bulk API.
Ignoring nextRecordsUrl and silently missing records.

quiz.q: How do you create-or-update by another system's key?
options: POST to create, then PATCH with the Salesforce Id if the POST fails
quiz.why: Upsert by external Id matches on that field.

quiz.q: A query returns 'done: false'. What next?
options: Follow nextRecordsUrl to get the next page
quiz.why: Results come in batches; follow nextRecordsUrl until done is true.

quiz.q: What bundles several REST calls into one request?
quiz.why: Composite reduces round trips.

nodes.title: Callouts from Apex
nodes.summary: Calling other systems, safely, from Salesforce.
nodes.lesson:
Outbound calls from Apex use `HttpRequest` and `Http.send()`:

- Point them at a **Named Credential** (`callout:Payments/charges`); the credential stores the URL and authentication (via an **External Credential**), so code holds no secrets.
- Callouts can't happen after uncommitted DML in the same transaction, and not synchronously from triggers: use **Queueable** with `Database.AllowsCallouts`.
- Set timeouts; check status codes; parse JSON into typed classes.
- In tests, `Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mock)` returns fake responses.
- **External Services** can generate invocable actions from an OpenAPI spec, so Flow can call an API with no code.
pitfalls: Secrets in code or custom settings.
Callout after DML: 'You have uncommitted work pending'.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. What should the Apex code reference instead of a URL and password?
options: A remote site setting with the password
quiz.why: Named Credentials keep endpoints and auth out of code.
quiz.imageAlt: Callout diagram: Apex calls a Named Credential that holds URL and auth.

quiz.q: A trigger needs to call an API. What do you do?
options: Enqueue a Queueable that implements Database.AllowsCallouts
Call it directly from the trigger with Http.send()
quiz.why: Callouts from triggers must be asynchronous.

quiz.q: What lets Flow call a REST API from an OpenAPI spec without code?
quiz.why: External Services turn an API spec into invocable actions.

nodes.diagramCaption: Callouts: Apex sends an HttpRequest to a Named Credential, which holds the URL and authentication and calls the external API.

nodes.title: Custom Apex APIs
nodes.summary: Building your own REST endpoints in Apex.
pitfalls: Exposing a class `without sharing` to an integration user that has broad access.
Returning 200 with an error message in the body.

quiz.q: Where are custom Apex REST endpoints served?
quiz.why: Apex REST lives under /services/apexrest/.

quiz.q: A client retries a POST after a timeout and two orders appear. What prevents this?
options: Idempotency: match on an external Id and upsert
quiz.why: Idempotent operations give the same result however often they run.

quiz.q: How should a custom endpoint report invalid input?
options: Set a 4xx status code with a clear message
Return 200 with an error message in the response body
quiz.why: Clients rely on status codes to know what happened.

nodes.title: Bulk data
nodes.summary: Loading and extracting millions of records.
nodes.lesson:
- **Bulk API 2.0** loads or queries large data sets asynchronously: create a job, upload CSV, close it, then poll for results and failed rows.
- It processes in batches on the server and counts far fewer API requests than one call per record.
- Turn off or bypass non-essential automation during big loads; sort data by parent to reduce lock contention.
- **Data Loader** uses the Bulk API under the hood when you switch it on.
concepts: Bulk API 2.0 jobs: create, upload, close, poll
pitfalls: Using the REST API one record at a time for a migration.
Not downloading the failed-rows file after a job.

quiz.q: Which API suits loading 2 million records?
quiz.why: Bulk API processes large volumes asynchronously.

quiz.q: After a Bulk job finishes, how do you find rows that failed?
options: They're emailed to the job's owner as a CSV
quiz.why: Each job provides successful and failed result files.

quiz.q: Why sort child records by parent before loading?
options: To reduce record-lock contention on the same parents
quiz.why: Children of one parent in different batches can fight over the parent's lock.

nodes.title: Events and change data capture
nodes.summary: Telling other systems what changed, as it happens.
nodes.lesson:
- **Platform events** are custom messages you publish (`Order_Shipped__e`) from Apex, Flow or external systems; subscribers react.
- **Change Data Capture (CDC)** publishes events automatically when records are created, updated, deleted or undeleted, for the objects you select.
- External systems subscribe through the **Pub/Sub API** (or CometD streaming) and can replay recent events after a disconnect.
- Events decouple systems: the publisher doesn't wait for, or even know about, the subscribers.
concepts: Change Data Capture for record changes
pitfalls: Polling an API every minute for changes when CDC would push them.
Assuming events are delivered exactly once: design subscribers to handle duplicates.

quiz.q: An external warehouse must learn about every Order update without polling. What fits?
quiz.why: CDC pushes record changes to subscribers.

quiz.q: What lets an external system catch up on events it missed while offline?
options: Data Loader, exporting the event object
Replay from a stored replay Id
quiz.why: Subscribers can replay events retained by the event bus.

quiz.q: Why design subscribers to handle duplicates?
options: Delivery is at least once, so the same event may arrive again
Events are never sent twice, so duplicates mean a bug
quiz.why: At-least-once delivery means idempotent handling.

nodes.title: Integration patterns
nodes.summary: Choosing the right approach for each integration.
nodes.lesson:
Most integrations fit a known pattern:

- **Request and reply**: Salesforce calls and waits (callout). Simple, but the user waits too.
- **Fire and forget**: send and move on (platform event, outbound message). Resilient, eventually consistent.
- **Batch data sync**: scheduled bulk moves of many records.
- **Remote call-in**: another system calls Salesforce's APIs.
- **UI update from data change**: push changes to listeners (CDC, streaming).
- **Data virtualisation**: show external data without copying it (Salesforce Connect, external objects).

Choose by who starts it, whether the caller must wait, how much data moves, and how fresh it must be.
concepts: Choosing by volume, timeliness and who initiates
pitfalls: Synchronous callouts for slow systems: users wait and transactions time out.
Copying huge external tables into Salesforce when they only need to be viewed.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. A large product catalogue lives in an ERP; users only need to view it in Salesforce. Which pattern?
quiz.why: Virtualisation shows external data without copying it.
quiz.imageAlt: Integration patterns diagram: Data virtualisation, 'External data shown, not copied'.

quiz.q: Using the diagram, which pattern sends a message and doesn't wait for an answer?
quiz.why: Fire and forget publishes and moves on.
quiz.imageAlt: Integration patterns diagram: Fire and forget, 'Send and move on (platform events)'.

quiz.q: Nightly, 500,000 records must move from Salesforce to a data warehouse. Which pattern?
quiz.why: Scheduled bulk movement is batch data sync.

nodes.diagramCaption: Six integration patterns: request and reply, fire and forget, batch data sync, remote call-in, UI update from data change, and data virtualisation.

nodes.title: Errors, retries and monitoring
nodes.summary: Keeping integrations working when things fail.
nodes.lesson:
Networks fail; design for it:

- **Retry** only what can succeed later (timeouts, `429`, `5xx`), with increasing delays; never retry `4xx` validation errors.
- Make writes **idempotent** so retries don't duplicate data.
- **Log** each exchange (without secrets) with a correlation Id that both systems record.
- Watch **limits**: daily API requests, concurrent long-running requests, callout timeouts.
- Alert on repeated failures instead of finding out from users.
concepts: Retry with backoff, only for retryable errors
pitfalls: Retrying in a tight loop and hitting rate limits harder.
Logging full request bodies that contain personal data or tokens.

quiz.q: Which response should be retried?
quiz.why: 503 is temporary; 4xx errors won't fix themselves.

quiz.q: What makes retries safe?
options: More API calls, sent in parallel
quiz.why: Idempotent operations can run twice with the same result.

quiz.q: What should integration logs never contain?
quiz.why: Logs are widely readable; credentials must stay out.

nodes.title: Salesforce Connect
nodes.summary: External objects: viewing data that stays outside.
nodes.lesson:
**Salesforce Connect** maps tables in another system to **external objects** (`Invoice__x`):

- Records are fetched live when users view them, not stored in Salesforce.
- Adapters: OData 2.0/4.0, cross-org, or a custom adapter written in Apex.
- External objects support lookups to and from Salesforce objects, SOQL (with some limits) and appear in list views and related lists.
- Good for large or rarely viewed data; not for data that needs heavy reporting or automation.
pitfalls: Expecting triggers and full reporting on external objects.

quiz.q: What suffix do external objects use?
quiz.why: External objects (Salesforce Connect) end in __x. __c is a custom object, __mdt custom metadata and __e a platform event.

quiz.q: Where does an external object's data live?
options: In the external system, fetched when viewed
Copied into Salesforce by a nightly sync job
quiz.why: Salesforce Connect reads it live.

quiz.q: Which is a poor fit for external objects?
options: Viewing records from a very large archive only occasionally
Data that needs heavy reporting and automation in Salesforce
quiz.why: Reporting and automation are limited on external objects.

nodes.title: Integration checkpoint
nodes.summary: Practise the PD II integration questions.
nodes.lesson: You can now authenticate systems, call out and be called, move bulk data, publish and subscribe to events, and choose a pattern. Practise the **integration** section of the PD II questions; for the full picture, the **Integration Architect** certification goes deeper into these designs.
concepts: Choosing and defending an integration design
pitfalls: Picking a tool before the pattern.
